title: PewCB One Desktop PCB fabrication system enables rapid prototyping at home
summary:
PewCB One is a desktop PCB prototyping system designed to accelerate hardware development by manufacturing PCBs at home or in the office in a few hours or less, instead of waiting days for a PCB to come back from the factory. Unlike desktop fabrication methods that rely on chemical processing, the PewCB One is more akin to a fully enclosed laser engraver housed with an integrated air filtration system. Users can perform the full process from double-sided PCB blanks to a complete PCBA at home. title: PyBLE open-source MicroPython IDE works over Bluetooth LE for tablet and iPad users
summary:
PyBLE is an open-source, MIT-licensed MicroPython IDE for programming microcontroller boards over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), which targets Android tablet and iPad users. PyBLE combines a Flutter-based IDE for iPad and Android with support for MicroPython and visual programming (Blockly), an open MicroPython agent firmware, and the PBLE/1 protocol fully documented by the developer. The IDE currently supports features such as editing and running Python, a live console, wireless file management, and initial firmware targets include ESP32, ESP32-S3, and ESP32-C3 wireless microcontrollers. PyBLE highlights: Flutter app Filtered BLE discovery and PBLE/1 open protocol support MicroPython editor with save, run, stop, soft reboot, and live console Wireless file browsing and transfer with integrity checks Offline Blockly workspace with GPIO and standard MicroPython NeoPixel blocks Editable beginner examples Exact Blockly sidecar reopening and a bounded Python-to-blocks importer Adaptive tablet interface for portrait and landscape use Local operation without an account, analytics, or [...]

title: Comu is a $6 tiny CH32V203 RISC-V development board that fits inside a USB port
summary:
Over the years, we have seen several tiny “omu” USB boards that share this “fits-in-a-USB-port” form factor. It started with the Tomu, based on a Silicon Labs EFM32 Cortex-M0+, followed by the Fomu with a Lattice iCE40 FPGA, Qomu with an EOS S3 Cortex-M4F MCU and FPGA, and the Somu, a tiny FIDO2 security key. Icy Electronics has now introduced Comu, another tiny development board based on the 144 MHz WCH CH32V203 RISC-V MCU. While measuring just 13 x 9.4 mm (slightly smaller than a microSD card), the board still packs two white LEDs, four capacitive touch buttons, and six GPIOs exposed through test pads. It is designed for bare-metal programming, custom USB HID projects, and USB packet experimentation. title: Elecrow ThinkNode M9 – A standalone ESP32-S3 MeshCore communication terminal with color LCD, QWERTY keyboard
summary:
Elecrow ThinkNode M9 is a standalone LoRa terminal that runs MeshCore firmware and features a QWERTY keyboard, color display, GPS, LoRa connectivity, and a 2,300mAh battery, making it suitable for outdoor and emergency communication. The device is built around an ESP32-S3R8 and a Semtech LR1110 LoRa module supporting US915 and EU868 frequencies, while the esp32-s3 adds Wi-Fi 4 and Bluetooth 5.0/BLE connectivity. Additionally, it features a 2.4-inch 240 × 320 TFT LCD, a 37-key physical QWERTY keyboard, GPS/GNSS support, plus a magnetic compass for navigation and location sharing. Other features include a USB-C port for charging and programming, RTC, buzzer, built-in antennas, and a 2,300mAh/3.8V Li-Po battery rated for up to 2–3 days in standby. The M9 targets outdoor exploration, emergency and disaster communication, remote operations, scientific research, and offline community or privacy-focused communication. title: Proxmox VE now officially supports 64-bit Arm (Aarch64) targets
summary:
Proxmox has recently announced the first official release of Proxmox Virtual Environment (VE) with support for 64-bit Arm (arm64/aarch64). Until now, the popular virtualization solution was only available for x86-64 (amd64). Proxmox VE 9.2 for arm64 is built on Debian 13.5 “Trixie” with Linux 7.0, and is otherwise based on the same code as the x86-64 version, and relies on the same configuration, tooling, and documentation, except for a few architecture-specific differences. The developers note that Proxmox VE for Arm fully supports NVIDIA Grace Hopper and NVIDIA Vera platforms, and “best-effort” support is available on other UEFI-based Armv8-A/Armv9-A hardware. However, device-tree-only single-board computers, such as the Raspberry Pi, are not supported, since the host must boot through UEFI and describe its hardware through ACPI. Having said that, we previously noted work on an UEFI+ACPI port for the Raspberry Pi 4, and users have already managed to have the release work [...]
